title: Âu Lạc
capsule: Âu Lạc was formed around 257 BCE when the Âu Việt chieftain Thục Phán conquered the Văn Lang kingdom of the Hùng kings and united the Âu Việt and Lạc Việt peoples, ruling from the capital Cổ Loa — a massive multi-walled citadel whose earthwork ramparts survive near modern Hanoi. The kingdom controlled a territory corresponding roughly to the Red River delta and adjacent highlands of northern Vietnam and parts of modern Guangxi. In 207 BCE the Chinese general Zhao Tuo (Triệu Đà) of the Qin-successor state of Nanyue conquered Âu Lạc through a combination of military force and political marriage alliance, absorbing it as two commanderies (Giao Chỉ and Cửu Chân) into the Nanyue realm.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Âu Lạc is semi-legendary; the Cổ Loa citadel provides archaeological grounding, but precise territorial boundaries are reconstructed from later Vietnamese and Chinese dynastic accounts and carry significant uncertainty.
